title: DHS Expands H-1B Fees to Extension Petitions, Adding Thousands in Costs for Employers
excerpt: A new federal rule effective September 9 requires covered employers to pay a $4,000 fee on H-1B extensions — previously charged only on initial petitions — as the legal battle over Trump's separate $100,000 visa fee continues in the courts.
body:
• DHS published a final rule on August 10 expanding the $4,000 "9-11 Biometric Fee" to cover H-1B extension petitions, not just initial filings — effective September 9, 2026
  • Covered employers (50+ employees, more than half on H-1B or L-1 visas) will see extension filing fees more than double, from $2,880 to $6,880 for a first H-1B extension
  • The rule arrives as Trump's separate $100,000 H-1B fee remains blocked after the First Circuit declined to stay a lower court ruling that struck it down in June
  • Immigration attorneys warn the combined fee pressure could force mid-size companies to rethink international hiring strategies

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security has published a final rule that significantly expands the scope of fees employers must pay when sponsoring H-1B workers, adding thousands of dollars in costs to visa extension petitions that were previously exempt.

The rule, published in the Federal Register on August 10 (91 FR 51360), extends the "9-11 Biometric Fee" — formally known as the Public Law 114-113 fee — to cover extension petitions filed on behalf of H-1B and L-1 visa holders. Since 2015, covered employers have been required to pay this fee only when filing initial petitions. Starting September 9, they must pay it on extensions as well.

What Changes and Who Pays

The fee amounts remain unchanged: $4,000 per H-1B petition and $4,500 per L-1 petition. But applying them to extensions transforms what was effectively a one-time cost into a recurring expense for every visa renewal cycle.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=qufyy0TOywg

For a covered employer filing a first H-1B extension, total filing fees will jump from $2,880 to $6,880 — an increase of nearly 140 percent. Second and subsequent extensions will rise from $1,380 to $5,380. The only exception: H-1B amendment petitions that do not request an extension of status.

"What was effectively a one-time fee of $4,000 per H-1B worker will now apply to almost every type of H-1B petition a covered employer will file."

— Buchalter LLP, immigration advisory

The rule applies to "covered employers" — companies with 50 or more U.S. employees where more than half hold H-1B or L-1 status. While the threshold shelters most large corporations (a 1,500-person company would need 750 H-1B or L-1 workers to qualify), it hits smaller and mid-size firms that rely heavily on visa workers, particularly IT staffing companies and multinational operations using L-1 intracompany transfers.

A Second Attempt at Fee Expansion

This is not the administration's first effort to broaden the fee. A similar expansion was attempted in August 2020 as part of a broader immigration fee overhaul but was enjoined by courts before taking effect. The Biden administration rescinded it in January 2024. DHS revived the effort through a notice of proposed rulemaking in June 2024, received 146 public comments, and published the final rule unchanged from the proposed version.

The Broader Fee Landscape

The extension fee expansion arrives against a backdrop of escalating H-1B costs and legal battles. Trump's separate $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions — imposed through a September 2025 presidential proclamation — was struck down by U.S. District Judge Leo Sorokin on June 8, who ruled it constituted an unlawful tax that Congress never authorized. The administration appealed, but the First Circuit Court of Appeals on July 24 declined to stay the lower court's ruling. USCIS has since updated its guidance to reflect that the $100,000 charge is not being collected.

The merits appeal on the $100,000 fee remains pending, leaving employers in legal limbo. Meanwhile, other H-1B costs have also risen: the electronic registration fee jumped from $10 to $215 for the fiscal year 2026 season, and premium processing now costs $2,965, up from $2,805.

Impact on Indian Tech Workers

Indian nationals account for the vast majority of H-1B visa recipients, making up roughly 72 percent of approved petitions in recent years. The fee increases disproportionately affect Indian-American-owned IT consulting and staffing firms, many of which meet the "covered employer" threshold and sponsor workers through multiple extension cycles.

"Enforcement against U.S. employers with nonimmigrant employees is on the rise and can be pursued through any one of the many regulatory schemes that touch on the employment of foreign nationals."

— Buchalter LLP

For workers already in the United States on H-1B status, the direct financial impact falls on their employers. But immigration attorneys caution that higher costs could lead some companies to decline extensions altogether, pushing workers toward self-transfer or departure.

What Employers Should Do Now

Immigration law firms are advising employers to audit their workforce composition immediately to determine whether they qualify as covered employers, assess the budget impact of extension fees on current and planned petitions, and review H-1B dependency status — a separate but related compliance requirement that can trigger additional attestation obligations.

The September 9 effective date leaves employers with less than three weeks to adjust filing strategies. Extensions filed before that date will not be subject to the expanded fee.
